title: Four sources, one answer
note: Al-Shafi'i ordered the sources of Islamic law into one shared grammar that jurists still argue by.

research.quotes: heroes.html#ash-shafii: 'ar-Risala, the Epistle: the first systematic book on usul al-fiqh... It set out the sources of law, Qur'an, the Sunnah... consensus, and analogy, and how they rank and interlock.' 'In 814 CE he moved to Egypt, and there did the thing scholars fear most: he publicly revised himself... his school transmits an old opinion and a new opinion side by side.' 'Before Shafi'i, brilliant jurists disagreed. After him, they disagreed by shared rules.'
research.retell: A jurist named Ash-Shafi'i figured out a fixed order for checking Islamic law, the Qur'an first, then the Prophet's example, then scholarly agreement, then similar cases, and judges still follow that same order today.

lines.text: Every Islamic ruling follows four steps
lines.sub: always in the same fixed order

lines.text: First, what does the Qur'an itself say
Then the Sunnah, the Prophet's practice
Then ijma, what the scholars agreed
Then qiyas, likeness to a case settled

lines.sub: after him, they disagreed by shared rules

lines.text: Every school of law still uses his four
He wrote the grammar for the argument
